headline: Wage catch-up scenario seen as least likely: weak unionization, profits concentrated in tech, and AI adoption substituting for rather than complementing labor continue to weigh on workers' bargaining power
reasoning: Three scenarios could resolve the gap between unit labor cost growth and core PCE inflation: wage catch-up (workers regain bargaining power, warranting further tightening), margin compression via slowing demand (disinflationary, no tightening needed), and cost-side margin compression from rising non-labor costs such as tariffs, energy, and AI infrastructure (a supply shock to be looked through). PIMCO views wage catch-up as the least likely scenario in the near term because unionization remains weak, higher profits are concentrated in tech company earnings, and AI adoption is a substitute for a broad range of tasks, which should continue to weigh on labor's bargaining power rather than restore it. Only the wage catch-up scenario implies the kind of labor-cost driven inflation persistence that monetary policy needs to guard against.

Inflation should cool, as input cost inflation fades.

headline: Above-target inflation is arithmetically a profit-share story, not a labor-cost story: ULC growth at ~1% YoY versus core PCE at 3.3%, with labor's share at its lowest since 1947
reasoning: Unit labor cost (ULC) growth is running at roughly 1% year-over-year, near the slowest pace since the pandemic, while core PCE is running at 3.3%. The gap is arithmetically explained by a decline in labor's share of income, which has fallen to its lowest level in the series since 1947. The mirror image shows up in profits: after-tax corporate profit margins as a percentage of gross value added are at their highest level in over 80 years, and S&P 500 net margins hit a record in the second quarter. This means today's above-target inflation is a profit-share story, not a labor-cost story, and monetary policy tightening aimed at cooling the labor market would not address the actual driver of inflation.
quote: Right now, the gap between ULC growth and core PCE is unusually wide. ULC growth is running at roughly a 1% year-over-year pace, near the slowest pace since the pandemic, while core PCE is running at 3.3%. That gap is arithmetically explained by the decline in labor's share or the rise in capital owner's share, which is the inverse of labor's share. And indeed, labor's share of income has fallen to the lowest level in the series since 1947. The mirror image shows up in profits. After-tax corporate profit margins as a percentage of gross value added were at their highest level in over 80 years of data, according to the national income and product accounts, while S&P 500 index net margins hit a record in the second quarter, according to fact-set data. In short, today's above-target inflation is arithmetically a profit-share story, not a labor-cost story.

We still expect core inflation to moderate over the coming months. headline: PIMCO views US Treasury buybacks as a useful liquidity tool that can reduce government borrowing costs over time without abandoning the 'regular and predictable' issuance framework.
reasoning: Tiffany Wilding argues that Treasury buybacks can improve market functioning and reduce borrowing costs by compressing the spread between Treasury yields and swap rates, which currently sits at 70 basis points at the 30-year point. The buybacks allow Treasury to act as a market maker of last resort — a role the Fed has sought to step away from — without fundamentally altering overall debt issuance levels, only the maturity mix. She notes that if Treasury increased T-bill share from 22% to 24% of outstanding debt, it could buy back up to $630 billion in the 10-to-30-year sector, rivalling past Fed QE programmes. However, Treasury's capacity is constrained compared to the Fed since buybacks must be financed through additional issuance. PIMCO believes this stable liquidity backstop, combined with other market structure improvements, supports Treasury's safe-haven status, as long as the regular and predictable auction framework is preserved.
quote: Our view is that buybacks can help with market functioning and reduce Treasury borrowing costs on average over time, especially if Treasury aims to establish itself as the new market maker of last resort, a role that the Federal Reserve has wanted to step away from. However, Treasury by itself can't completely alter the fundamentals that drive longer-term Treasury pricing. Complementing regular and predictable issuance by providing a well-understood, stable liquidity backstop to guard against bouts of market dysfunction should be positive for the market. Currently, Treasury funds itself at 5.2% at the 30-year point on the curve. That's 70 basis points above the similar maturity fixed rate swap, according to Treasury and Bloomberg data. There is a lot of room for Treasury, through enhanced market liquidity policies, to compress that rate for better funding levels for the government.

headline: PIMCO warns that departing from 'regular and predictable' Treasury issuance would raise term premiums and increase government borrowing costs, citing the 1970s as a cautionary tale.
reasoning: Wilding recounts how Treasury's tactical, opportunistic coupon offerings in the 1970s repeatedly surprised investors and caused market disarray, such as the March 1975 episode where simultaneous Treasury and corporate bond issuance destabilised the bond market. Since the 1980s, recurring standardised auctions have reduced yield volatility on Treasury financing days. She emphasises that Treasury is too large to time markets credibly, and that moving away from a predictable framework would increase issuance uncertainty, raise term premiums, and directly undermine Treasury's debt-cost minimisation goals. PIMCO doubts Treasury is abandoning this framework despite the buyback announcement, noting Treasury has repeatedly stated it does not react to short-term rate levels.
quote: While regular and predictable is not the only driver of long-end term premiums, moving away from this strategy would likely come with higher issuance uncertainty and Treasury market volatility and would tend to increase term premiums over time. It's a strategy that directly goes against Treasury's debt-cost minimization goals. As Treasury itself has said on multiple occasions, it is too big to time a market that it relies on for U.S. government funding. A regular, predictable, yet flexible framework that is well understood by markets should serve everyone well.

headline: PIMCO flags hyperscaler AI-related debt issuance as a crowding-out factor creating indigestion in the bond market

PIMCO characterises this as bond market indigestion — too much issuance too fast — but notes there may be some price sensitivity at the margin and that it is well-heralded and therefore likely not a permanent disruptor of the yield range.
quote: I think it's indigestion. I think we've had a moment in time that is unique in its in the scale and scope of issuance across the hyperscalers. And I think the market is suffering from some indigestion. I mean they're still super high-quality companies but even their credit default swap spreads an indication of you know their credit worthiness have increased as well as yields and term premium have increased. So I do think that there is a meaningful impact there and I would say it's you know as simple as indigestion. I think there's a real question as to whether or not the hyperscalers are investing like gangbusters and that investing has gone from free cash flow to now debt financed. I think there's an open question as to whether or not there's some price sensitivity there.

headline: PIMCO views US Treasury buyback announcement as sensible and atypical policy intervention to prevent disorderly long-end yields
reasoning: When the 30-year real rate broke 3%, the US Treasury announced buyback auctions and a shift in issuance from long-dated to shorter-dated maturities, which PIMCO views as atypical but sensible. The Treasury is effectively stepping back from validating high financing costs at the long end and allowing hyperscalers to issue there instead. This is comparable to coordinated yen intervention — not aimed at fixing a price or repressing rates, but at preventing disorderly conditions that would directly harm American households through mortgage and other borrowing markets. This is not without precedent in prior Treasury vintages.

It's the actual opposite because we're buying back not forcing people to own. And we're not gonna let longer-term yields become disorderly because that has a very direct impact on American households whether it be through the mortgage market or other other borrowing markets. And that's perfectly reasonable in terms of a policy.

headline: PIMCO argues AI is likely bond-bullish over the medium term, lowering neutral rates via precautionary savings and improved fiscal expectations despite popular narrative of AI raising R-Star.
reasoning: Contrary to the prevailing central banker consensus that AI will push neutral rates higher, PIMCO's event study analysis finds that long-dated real and nominal yields have consistently fallen around major AI model releases since 2023. Cumulative yield changes on the 43 days of significant AI model releases were roughly 100 basis points lower, meaning yields would have risen 200bps over the period if AI release days were excluded. The mechanism proposed is twofold: first, AI creates economic disruption and labor displacement uncertainty, prompting households to increase precautionary savings and demand for safe assets, which puts downward pressure on neutral rates; second, stronger AI-driven productivity growth raises the long-run tax base and improves fiscal sustainability, compressing term premia on government bonds. PIMCO notes this dynamic distinguishes the current episode from the late 1990s tech cycle, where innovation was broadly labor-augmenting and income gains were widespread, whereas current AI gains appear more narrowly distributed to capital holders, amplifying precautionary behavior. Term premia compression explains around half of the overall decline in long-term yields around AI model releases, per a Federal Reserve Board staff model analysis.
quote: AI is widely expected to push neutral rates higher, but we're seeing market-based evidence that points in the opposite direction. While market reactions could shift over time, these dynamics at a minimum complicate the current policy narrative. Even if AI ultimately raises trend growth, its near-to-medium term impact may be to increase the demand for safe assets, compress term premia, and lower real neutral rates. In other words, AI may be bond bullish over the medium term, lowering neutral rates via precautionary savings and improved fiscal expectations, even as it raises longer-run growth potential.
episode_title: Does AI Raise or Lower Neutral Rates?

quote: Our view is that probably two cuts this year. And then there's a scenario where there's a third cut that can happen, but unlikely to see too much more in the very near term.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO warns elevated equity valuations (CAPE ~35) imply near-zero median returns over next 3-5 years
reasoning: Mittal notes that historically, starting equity valuations at current cyclically-adjusted PE levels near 35 have corresponded to median forward returns close to 0% over three to five years, driven by valuation correction risk. He also flags concentration risk in AI/hyperscaler names and parallels to prior CAPEX cycles (railroads, telecoms) that saw significant consolidation.
quote: Quickly adjusted PEs are near 35. And whenever you have started with these valuations, again, this time can be different, but on average, the median return in equities when you have started with this valuation has been near 0%.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: Sees select value in investment-grade corporates and bank credits while running near-zero exposure to loans and high yield
reasoning: While acknowledging complacency in lower-quality credit, Mittal says select opportunities in senior investment-grade corporates and bank names still look interesting. The team is also positioning for anticipated sizeable AI-sector bond issuance in 2025 as an opportunistic entry point.
quote: Select opportunities in senior, in investment grade corporates, banks, still look interesting and then continuing to work with our specialist team to source one off transactions. We expect a pre sizable issuance in the AI space this year.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO likes senior structured products including AAA ABS and AAA CLO tranches as part of core positioning
reasoning: In the current credit environment where the team is cautious on lower-quality credit, Mittal highlights triple-A rated ABS and CLO exposures as areas where value remains without taking on undue credit risk.
quote: We still like senior structured products. Triple A B S exposures, triple A C L O.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO reduced US curve steepener (5s/30s) from sizable position to near-neutral after 5/30 spread widened to ~120bps
reasoning: PIMCO had been running a large curve steepener for roughly 12 months based on deficit concerns and expected Fed intervention. After the 5/30 spread widened from near-zero to ~120bps by October/November, the team judged valuations had adjusted significantly, positioning had become more consensus, and the Treasury could shift issuance patterns, reducing conviction in the steepener.
quote: What we have done in core strategies is just reduce that magnitude depending upon the strategy to either closer to neutral or to a much smaller steepener.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO running near-zero exposure to leveraged loans and high yield, warns of complacency and elevated software concentration risk in private credit
reasoning: Mittal argues that post-GFC excess returns in levered credit of 4-5% per year have bred complacency and excess leverage at the issuer level. Software now represents up to 20-25% of some private direct lending funds, creating concentration risk from AI disruption. On a forward basis, excess returns in loans and private direct lending are expected to be meaningfully below current headline yields.
quote: In our view, you know, likely on a go forward basis, if we think about it next three to five years, we think excess returns in those markets, the levered loans, as well as in the call it the broad, as well as in the private direct lending space would be much lower than what the initial spreads or the initial yields might indicate.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO running small short US dollar position in core strategies on secular weakening view, while affirming reserve currency status
reasoning: Mittal believes the dollar is modestly overvalued on a secular basis and has positioned with a small underweight, but is explicit that this does not reflect concern about dollar reserve currency status. He notes the traditional safe-haven bid for the dollar in risk-off episodes remains intact over a 25-year history, though very recent data post-April has been mixed.
quote: We are running in core strategies some, some, some underweight dollar, some short dollar position. But that does not, in any shape or form means that we are concerned about the safety of the dollar or dollar as a reserve currency.
episode_title: Don’t Ignore Your Core: Process and Progress with PIMCO CIO Mohit Mittal

headline: PIMCO prefers the belly of the curve (~5-year maturities) over long-end bonds, but sees opportunity to extend duration into long-end as yields remain elevated
reasoning: PIMCO ran a steepener trade in 2025, overweighting ~5-year instruments and significantly underweighting the long end. Long-end yields have not rallied as the short end has, creating an opportunity in 2026 to selectively extend duration into longer maturities, where government bond yields in high-quality markets are approaching 5% or higher. Cash rates are expected to decline, increasing the cost of staying in cash.
quote: Those longer maturities that we were underweight haven't gone down at all and across many markets have actually gone up creating what may very well be an opportunity in 2026 to extend some of those maturities and areas that are now offering yields well above the Bloomberg aggregate index in government bond markets, high quality markets like ours, almost 5% type yields.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO sees compelling opportunity in global sovereign bonds outside the US, including Australia, UK and high-quality EM, offering superior yield, credit quality and diversification
reasoning: Ivascyn argues that many non-US countries have stronger fiscal positions than the US yet offer higher yields, creating a rare combination of pick-up in yield, credit quality and diversification. Australia and the UK are cited as examples. High-quality EM sovereigns, which got ahead of inflation post-COVID, offer very high real interest rates. Currency hedging is available for risk management, but a weaker USD trend over the next few years is also an expected tailwind.
quote: Australia is a good example. The UK which has the challenges associated with a smaller open economy and their own currency, but they too offer quite attractive yields versus the United States... higher quality emerging markets well ahead of the curve on managing inflation coming out of the covid period offer very very high real interest rates.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO base case sees Fed cutting to ~3% but views 100bp of easing as excessive; maintains neutral positioning on rate direction
reasoning: Ivascyn characterises the Fed as dovishly inclined and likely to remain so under a new chair, with a base case of rates moving toward 3%. However, he sees the bar for rate hikes as high and believes that betting on 100bp of cuts is excessive given strong recent data and inflation remaining above target. PIMCO is not making outsized positioning bets relative to current curve pricing.
quote: We do believe this is a dovishly inclined Fed... our base case thinking is that there'll be enough economic weakness in the base case for the Fed to get rates down towards 3%... betting on a hundred basis points of cuts right now is a bit excessive at least in terms of base case thinking.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO remains cautious on corporate credit, viewing spreads as tight and credit quality deteriorating even as the base case remains constructive
reasoning: Ivascyn notes that corporate credit will likely perform in a positive growth base case, but finds the asset class less interesting given tight spreads and ongoing credit quality deterioration. He sees a decent amount of complacency, particularly in lower-quality segments, and believes PIMCO strategies can match or exceed credit-heavy strategies via higher-quality alternatives without taking on the same economic sensitivity.
quote: Credits done very very well. There's a decent amount of complacency in this market. Under any quality continues to deteriorate so again, we're not screaming from the rooftops like we were in the mid-2000s... we just find it less interesting.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO warns private credit faces elevated losses from AI-driven disruption and a widening gap between public and private market valuations
reasoning: Ivascyn highlights two risks: first, publicly traded vehicles holding private credit or real estate are weakening, and the gap between their marked-up private valuations and public market prices creates a risk of forced selling and credit widening; second, AI-driven disruption is causing strain in direct lending and senior secured loan spaces even in a strong macro environment, as borrowers in older economy sectors are being displaced. Losses are expected to be higher than investors have grown accustomed to post-GFC.
quote: If growth is being fueled by highly disruptive new technologies, what may work for the economy as a whole can be quite detrimental for certain segments of the older economy... I think some of the strain and stress you've seen in the direct lending space even in the senior secured loan space is associated with these early stages of technological disruption.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO urges investors to reduce excess cash holdings as cash rates decline and longer-maturity bond yields remain attractive
reasoning: Ivascyn argues that the cost of holding cash has risen as the yield give-up versus intermediate bonds has widened and is likely to grow further as the Fed cuts rates toward 3%. He encourages investors who stayed in cash after the 2022 bond drawdown to consider extending duration modestly, as the combination of still-attractive yields and expected Fed easing makes bonds more compelling on a risk-adjusted basis than cash.
quote: Cash rates are probably going lower. The Fed wants to get them lower. We think they get down to at least 3%. But the cost of holding cash has steadily gone up the last year or two while yields have remained quite attractive in longer maturities... even from a defensive perspective, the idea of extending out the curve a little bit, extending into a longer maturity, finding you don't have to go all the way up to 30 years, likely makes a lot of sense.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO sees US growth accelerating in H1 2026 driven by AI/tech capex and Trump tax cut consumer boost, but expects the optimism is largely priced into markets
reasoning: Ivascyn expects positive US growth with an acceleration in H1 2026, driven by infrastructure/tech investment and the delayed consumer impact of Trump's tax cuts. However, he notes that this optimism is already reflected in equity and credit valuations, so PIMCO is only marginally more cautious than market pricing implies. The consumer boost from tax cuts is seen as temporary, while the infrastructure spend trajectory is more uncertain.
quote: We're continuing to be pretty optimistic about the growth picture. And in fact, we see growth accelerating in the first half of the year here in the United States... this type of optimism that we have is reflected in market pricing, right? Whether you're looking at equities or credit that the riskier areas of the market.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO expects the US dollar to continue weakening over the next few years and holds modest non-dollar exposure as a diversifier
reasoning: Ivascyn notes the dollar weakened significantly in H1 2025 and expects that trend to continue over the next few years, albeit in a bumpy fashion. PIMCO does not hold a large non-dollar allocation but sees currency diversification as a source of incremental return and portfolio volatility reduction.
quote: The dollar weakened quite significantly during the first half of last year. We expect over the course of the next few years the dollar weakening trend to continue. It'll be bumpy. We don't have a tremendous amount of non-dollar exposure across most of our portfolios, but a great source of diversification.
episode_title: Dan Ivascyn: Beyond the Base Case in 2026

headline: PIMCO recommends broad commodity exposure including gold as a portfolio diversifier and hedge against fiscal/currency risks in 2026
reasoning: Gold has risen over 50% in 2025, partly driven by central banks now owning more gold than Treasuries. While on a risk-adjusted basis PIMCO sees bonds as marginally more attractive than gold based on real yield metrics, gold should continue to perform well. A broader commodity allocation acts as a hedge against energy liabilities for households and against dollar depreciation.
quote: A broader exposure to real assets, commodities more generally, to us is a prudent strategy... central banks now own more gold than they own treasuries... it's creating a little bit of that richness.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO prefers mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities over corporate credit given more attractive relative valuations
reasoning: Investment grade and high-yield corporate credit spreads are in the lowest decile of attractiveness over the past decade, with a lot of good economic news already priced in. By contrast, MBS and ABS offer better risk-adjusted yields. PIMCO has been heavily invested in these sectors and, while the valuation gap has narrowed, it persists.
quote: We've been heavily invested in either mortgage-backed securities or asset-backed securities because their valuations have looked much more attractive to us... there's still a gap and so we'd much rather have the security of a mortgage or an asset-backed security versus unsecured corporate credit at a more attractive yield spread or risk premium.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO issues strong call to action to move out of cash into 2–5 year high-quality fixed income before further Fed rate cuts erode money market yields
reasoning: With $8 trillion sitting in money market funds and T-bill yields already fallen from 5.25% to ~3.75%, PIMCO expects the Fed to continue cutting toward 2.75–3% by end-2026. A double-A minus, 3–3.5 year duration portfolio currently yields 6.5%, offering a compelling lock-in opportunity. The stock-bond correlation has also turned favourable again, adding diversification benefit.
quote: There's plenty of portfolios I run a portfolio that is double-A minus average credit quality... three to three and a half years of duration so right in the sweet spot of the yield curve and it yields six and a half percent... the answer to your question is absolutely not — there's plenty of opportunity... if you're still sitting in cash at the end of 2026 you might very well be disappointed with your results.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO sees supportive but valuation-stretched backdrop for US equities in 2026, favouring value over momentum
reasoning: PIMCO expects US growth of around 2% in 2026 (trend-like) with moderating inflation, which is a broadly fine backdrop for equities. However, valuation remains elevated — particularly for large-cap tech — with mid-to-upper 30x PE ratios. The firm recommends rotating toward value factors and broadening geographic exposure rather than chasing momentum in already expensive indices.
quote: Our only concern about equities is that valuation continues to look a little bit stretched... 2026 could very well be another pretty good year for equity investors but we'd make a few points there — one would be that again the starting point of valuation... is certainly elevated.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO is short the long end of the yield curve, preferring 2–5 year maturities as fiscal dominance risks steepen the curve globally
reasoning: Despite Fed cuts at the short end, 10-year yields have risen since September — a pattern visible in Australia and the UK as well — reflecting fiscal dominance and debt/deficit concerns. PIMCO's flexible portfolios are actually short long-duration bonds and prefers 2–5 year maturities which are anchored by central bank policy rather than unanchored by poor fiscal dynamics.
quote: I'm blessed with the ability to run a flexible portfolio that is actually short the long end of the curve... we'd definitely not — for individuals and for advisors — stick to those two to five year maturities because they are anchored by a Federal Reserve that's going to continue to lower short-term interest rates rather than unanchored by poor debt and deficit dynamics.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO sees attractive after-tax yields in high-quality municipal bonds for taxable investors, though cautions against reaching for yield in lower-quality project finance
reasoning: Munis lagged badly around Liberation Day and through the summer but have recovered. After-tax yields remain very attractive for high-tax-bracket investors, with strong state-level fundamentals driven by elevated tax receipts. PIMCO warns against high-yield muni exposure where project finance has created episodic credit problems, and recommends active management to capture the opportunity.
quote: There's no doubt that munis, particularly as part of a wealthy household or high tax bracket household, they've lagged and the after-tax yields look super attractive... you don't have to go too far down in credit quality to get a really attractive after-tax yield.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO flags risk that AI capex cycle shifts from free-cash-flow-funded to debt-funded, potentially pressuring high-flying tech valuations
reasoning: Much of the current AI investment cycle has been funded out of free cash flow, which differentiates it from the dot-com era. However, PIMCO sees a risk that in 2026 some companies may need to shift to debt financing to sustain capital expenditure, which combined with already elevated valuations could deteriorate fundamentals. The firm notes CDS spreads have already widened for at least one major participant as an 'anti-AI hedge'.
quote: One of the questions will be — to fund this massive amount of capital expenditure — will that shift at some point in 2026 from free cash flow to requiring a bit of debt financing and leverage... starting with high valuation and perhaps deteriorating fundamentals even though there's this great hope of AI.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO urges global equity diversification as US index concentration in mega-cap tech leaves investors underexposed to cheaper international markets
reasoning: The major US indices have become increasingly concentrated in a narrow set of high-valuation stocks. International and global equities offer mid-to-upper teens PE multiples with supportive macro backdrops of trend-like growth, moderating inflation, and central banks continuing to cut rates. PIMCO recommends intentionally broadening exposure beyond US index-heavy positions.
quote: Looking around the world to diversify globally... the indexes has narrowed your exposure to equities and so you may need as an advisor maybe in a call to intentionally broaden out your exposure to other parts of the market.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO warns on private direct lending: floating-rate exposure, tightening spreads, deteriorating SME fundamentals and illiquidity make risk/reward unattractive versus public alternatives
reasoning: Direct lending was attractive when rates were rising from zero, but with rates now falling, floating-rate coupons are declining while spreads have narrowed and underwriting discipline has eroded. Small and medium enterprises show rising stress — 11.4% of the cohort are paying interest-in-kind. Publicly traded BDCs trade at meaningful discounts to par, suggesting private portfolios are overmarked. PIMCO sees this resolving through a more realistic marking of portfolios in 2026.
quote: 11.4% of companies in that cohort are now picking on their debt — they're paying in kind... publicly traded alternative asset management firms have their equities done poorly this year... the markets telling us they don't want to pay a dollar, they want to pay 90 cents or 85 cents to access that cash flow stream.
episode_title: Charting the Year Ahead with Marc Seidner

headline: PIMCO recommends staying up in quality, maintaining liquidity, and avoiding cyclicals such as chemicals and autos as late-cycle credit stress builds.
reasoning: Cyclical sectors like chemicals and autos are already showing pressure and cracks are emerging. Against a backdrop of tight spreads, declining coupons in floating rate instruments, and uncertain economic conditions, the risk-reward of lower quality credit is unattractive. Active management with rotation in and out of sectors is preferred over passive capital deployment strategies.
quote: In general we're preaching stay up in quality stay liquid be careful the cyclicals right now you know as an example there not everything is terrible.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: PIMCO warns private credit is showing late-cycle stress with shadow default rates around 6%, rising PIK income and amendments, and concerns about underwriting standards.
reasoning: The rapid growth of private credit to nearly $2 trillion has been accompanied by looser underwriting standards and weaker deals. Shadow default rates for private credit are around 6% according to Lincoln data, significantly higher than high yield's sub-2% and bank loans' 3-4%. PIK income now represents around 12% of total BDC income, more than double levels from a few years ago, signalling deteriorating credit quality.
quote: Their shadow default rate for private credit is around 6% today so pretty elevated especially as you kind of contrast that to you know high yield has been sub 2% default rate for the last couple of years.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: High yield default rates remain benign at sub-2% and the index has gravitated toward higher quality double-B issuers, making it relatively more resilient than bank loans or private credit.
reasoning: High yield has maintained sub-2% default rates over the last couple of years with the same level forecast into 2026. The index has shifted toward a more double-B oriented, higher-quality composition over time. However, recovery rates across high yield have also deteriorated below historical averages, which is a concern in stress scenarios.
quote: High yield has been sub 2% default rate for the last couple of years. That's even our forecast out to 26.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: Bank loan default rates hovering near historical average of 3-4% but recovery rates have collapsed to below 40 cents on the dollar, well below the historical 60-80 cents.
reasoning: Bank loans sit between high yield and private credit in terms of default risk, with rates near the historical 3-4% average. However, loan recovery rates on an LTM basis have fallen below 40 cents, the sixth consecutive year below historical averages, driven by more loan-only issuers with less subordination, weaker covenants, and liability management exercises that pit creditors against each other.
quote: The bank loan recovery is less than 40 cents on an LTM basis today and historically that would be you know 60 to 80 cents so well below and I think it's the sixth consecutive year that it's come in below historical average.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: PIMCO constructive on real estate broadly and high-end consumer credit, seeing value in sectors that have already gone through restructuring pressure.
reasoning: Sectors like telecom and healthcare that went through restructuring or stress a couple of years ago have come out in a decent position. PIMCO is broadly constructive on real estate and focuses on high-end consumer collateral, particularly pools backed by homeowners whose net worth advantage over non-homeowners is as wide as it has ever been.
quote: Mentioned the REITs and I think that we're constructive by and large on real estate that so yeah any you know on the high end consumer the consumer that owns a house there definitely places to find value within the market.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: PIMCO flags technology concentration in credit portfolios—representing 15-30% of BDC and bank loan exposure—as a major looming risk due to AI disruption and poor recovery prospects.
reasoning: Technology, particularly enterprise software, represents 15-20% of the bank loan market and around 20-30% of BDC portfolios. AI deployment poses a significant disruption risk to software-as-a-service business models that were previously considered predictable and asset-light. Recovery rates in a technology bankruptcy would likely be very low due to obsolescence risk, making this a key credit concern going into 2026.
quote: If you think about 30% of the BDCs or 20 of 30% round numbers are kind of exposed to technology I think that's a big looming risk because we just don't know how it's gonna play out yet as AI gets deployed does it disrupt does it dislocate and I would expect your recoveries to be pretty pretty nasty if you get the bankruptcy because there's just obsolescence risk.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: PIMCO favours asset-based finance over corporate direct lending as better relative value today, though warns the trade is becoming increasingly crowded.
reasoning: Asset-based finance offers better relative value compared to corporate credit given compressed spreads and deteriorating underwriting in direct lending. PIMCO has deep institutional expertise in verifying collateral and conducting diligence, which many newer entrants to the space lack. The firm focuses on high-quality consumer collateral pools, particularly homeowner-backed assets. However, the space is becoming crowded as private credit managers pivot toward it.
quote: As a firm we're definitely favoring asset-based financing as a better relative value trade today but with the caveat it's becoming also a little bit of a crowded trade.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: Public BDCs trading at an average 9% discount to NAV, reflecting concerns about dividend cuts from base rate compression and fundamental credit deterioration.
reasoning: BDC prices sold off significantly following recent private credit bankruptcies and have only partially recovered. They are trading at an average 9% discount to NAV, reflecting the dual headwinds of declining dividends as short rates fall and rising credit concerns. The discount signals the market does not value underlying loan portfolios at their manager-stated marks.
quote: The BDCs traded off pretty significantly they've retraced a little bit in recent weeks but they're still trading on average if you look at the broad index at a 9% discount.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets

headline: PIMCO expects solid credit market surface returns in 2026 but sees significant dispersion and elevated defaults beneath the surface, particularly in lower-quality borrowers.
reasoning: Spreads are expected to look similar to today on the surface, but dispersion and bifurcation will increase with elevated defaults, especially among lower-quality borrowers with less liquidity. The economic base case is a mild slowdown, not a major recession, but uncertainty around tariffs and Fed policy adds risk. Active management and rotating in and out of positions will be critical to navigating this environment.
quote: We should anticipate spreads on the surface to look similar to where they are today but beneath the surface a lot of dispersion a lot of bifurcation elevated defaults you know particular focus on some of the lower quality borrowers where there's less liquidity.
episode_title: Will Headlines Hit Your Bottom Line? Risk and Reality in Today’s Credit Markets
